title: Thematic Analysis Coding Laboratory
summary: Six invented interview extracts about asking for help at university, worked one at a time. The learner writes a code of their own, optionally borrows from a bank of six candidate codes that each explain what they do rather than whether they are right, and then sets their reading beside three defensible coding passes over the same words - semantic, latent and situated. Each extract closes with a reflexive prompt about what the reader brought with them. Nothing is scored, and inter-rater agreement is explicitly not the criterion.
learningObjectives: Describe coding in reflexive thematic analysis as an analytic act rather than an extraction.
Produce both semantic and more interpretive codes for the same extract.
State what a given coding decision brings forward and what it pushes out of view.
Distinguish a code from a filing category and from an imported theoretical diagnosis.
Articulate assumptions brought to an extract before coding it.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; anything typed stays in the browser tab, is never compared with anyone else's, and nothing is inferred about the person using the tool.
accessibilityNotes: Native text input, select, checkboxes and buttons, each with an explicit label and grouped in a fieldset with a legend. There are no charts: every output is text, so no visual-only information exists to be paired. The extract and the learner's own code are pinned to the top of the stage so the words being coded stay visible while the coding controls beside them are used. Each of the three coding passes names its own level in the heading and prints what it brings forward and what it puts in the background as labelled sentences, so the coloured left border is a redundant cue; each bank code prints its level as text above the label. Progress is shown in a stage track that marks the current and compared extracts with visually hidden text as well as styling. Changes announce full sentences through the polite live region, focus moves to the laboratory heading when it opens, forced-colours rules are provided, and the layout is usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Coding as an analytic act: three defensible readings of the same six extracts, and no answer key
simulationNotes: Six short interview extracts invented for teaching, attributed to fictional students of varying year and background, on the topic of asking for help at university. The same fictional dataset is used by the Theme or Topic challenge and the Reflexivity and Alternative Theme Builder in this module, so the three tools can be run as a sequence. Nothing is scored: the tool never marks a code right or wrong and never computes agreement between codings, and the page states why inter-rater agreement is not the criterion for reflexive thematic analysis. Each extract carries a bank of six candidate codes tagged semantic, latent or situated, each with a written note on what that code does and what it costs - including, deliberately, codes that would not survive scrutiny, such as a theoretical construct imported wholesale and a category label that files the extract without saying anything about it. Three coding passes are supplied per extract, chosen to make the semantic-to-situated range visible; they are not the three possibilities, and the debrief says a narrative, psychosocial or feminist reading would produce others. Free text typed by the learner is echoed back without evaluation and is never stored or transmitted.
